entries.title: Ukraine launches major drone attack on Russia’s Moscow region, killing two
entries.summary: Russia says 290 drones targeted Moscow and nearby regions in the overnight Ukrainian assault.
entries.content:
Russia says 290 drones targeted Moscow and nearby regions in the overnight Ukrainian assault.

Ukraine has launched a major drone attack on Moscow, killing two people and setting fire to a warehouse in the capital city, Russian officials say.

Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on Tuesday that the overnight assault involved 650 drones heading towards the city, most of which were shot down, as both sides intensify long-range strikes on infrastructure before winter.

Regional Governor Andrei Vorobyov said one person was killed in Radumlya and another was killed in Barbybino. He said seven people had been injured and that 47 houses, four apartments and three cars had been damaged.

He said 185 drones were “destroyed or neutralised” over the wider region.

Prominent war blogger Yuri Podolyaka said an oil storage tank was hit at the Volodarskaya oil storage and distribution facility, the biggest in the Moscow region. The facility stores diesel, petrol and jet fuel. There was no official confirmation that it had been hit.

Volodarskaya is one of the major hubs in the distribution system of Transneft and is linked to Moscow’s main oil refinery. It supplies fuel to all three of the capital’s large airports.

Ukraine has increasingly targeted oil refineries, depots and export terminals in ⁠an effort to deprive Moscow of the revenues it needs to ⁠finance the war that Russia began in February 2022.

Reporting from Moscow, Al Jazeera’s Dmitry Medvenko said the attack ended a relative lull in large Ukrainian strikes on Moscow since September 20.

Separately on Tuesday, a Ukrainian drone attack on a minibus in the Russian-occupied part of the Ukrainian Zaporizhia region killed three people, Moscow-installed authorities said.

Russia has recently intensified ⁠attacks on the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, sending waves of missiles and drones by night and day. Its latest targets have included bridges across the Dnipro River.

Kremlin-appointed official Yevgeny Balitsky said on Telegram that a Ukrainian drone hit the minibus close to a village near the front line, killing “three people, including the driver” and wounding three passengers.

Both Russia and Ukraine have increased strikes in the fifth year of the war, with diplomacy so far failing to end fighting and the United Nations warning of a significant rise in civilian deaths.

entries.title: Francis Halzen wins Nobel Prize in Physics for work on ‘ghost particles’
entries.summary: Belgian physicist worked to build Antarctic observatory that tracks neutrinos from deep space.
entries.content:
Belgian physicist worked to build Antarctic observatory that tracks neutrinos from deep space.

Belgian physicist Francis Halzen has won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for creating a giant detector in Antarctica that captures neutrinos, the so-called “ghost particles” from space that scientists believe offer clues to how the universe evolved.

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the prestigious award in Stockholm on Tuesday, crediting Halzen with a central role in building the IceCube Neutrino Observatory.

The neutrino interactions collected by the observatory provide information about how high-energy neutrinos are created and may even reveal previously unknown phenomena, the Academy said.

“It was a great surprise, and I obviously didn’t expect it,” Halzen said, speaking to the committee by phone from Italy, in a call broadcast at the news conference to announce the winner.

The 82-year-old said it was predicted before that he would win the Nobel Prize, but the announcement still made him feel “strange”.

“I am working on a proposal, and I hope that this prize will help getting it approved,” he said to chuckles from the audience.

‘Information from the cosmos’

Neutrinos have nearly no mass and carry no electric charge, so they can cross between planets, stars and human bodies without being altered, making them rare and hard to catch. There are roughly 100 trillion solar and cosmic neutrinos that pass through our bodies every second.

Halzen first proposed the IceCube project in 1988, realising that the clear ice beneath the South Pole could act as a detector, so on the rare occurrence a neutrino strikes an atomic nucleus, it gives off a flash of light that buried sensors can record.

Richard Fitzgerald, editor-in-chief of Physics Today, said although hundreds of people built the observatory, it “all started with one person”, noting that the physics prize has rarely gone to one sole winner in recent years.

“People joined him in the quest for these neutrino messengers. The messenger is bringing information from cosmos,” committee member Eva Olsson said during the news conference. “They opened the door to distant galaxies and tell us about the processes of exploding stars.”

Eva Lindroth, a researcher in Stockholm and a member of the Nobel Committee, told Al Jazeera that Halzen’s observatory has helped scientists understand high-energy particles.

“The nice thing with neutrinos is that they come straight at us,” she said. “That way we can ultimately understand these sources of high-energy particles and understand more about how things in the universe, like how galaxies are formed and the roles of the black holes in that process.

“It gives a new way to study the universe,” Lindroth added. “They give us information which we cannot get in any other way.”

Last year’s award went to John Clarke, Michel Devoret and John Martinis for experiments on quantum physics.

On Monday, the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded to two American scientists for discoveries that helped explain how the brain works.

The next award will be the Nobel Prize in Chemistry, which will be announced on Wednesday in Stockholm.

Nobel laureates will receive their awards in a ceremony on December 10, marking the anniversary of Swedish chemist Alfred Nobel, who established the award; members of the royal families of Sweden and Norway will be in attendance.

entries.title: Mapping where US bombers are based globally
entries.summary: The US has pulled its B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford amid Iran fears. Here's where else they can fly from.
entries.content:
The US has pulled its B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford amid Iran fears. Here’s where else they can fly from.

Over the course of Sunday, a dozen B-1B bombers took off from Royal Air Force (RAF) Fairford in western England and flew home to the United States. Their departure abruptly ended the base’s role as a launchpad for US strikes on Iran, which began on February 28.

The base, roughly 160km (100 miles) west of London, is the US Air Force’s only European airfield for heavy bombers and a key forward operating location for deployed bombers.

Over the past two weeks, six people were arrested on suspicion of “terrorism”. They were all released on bail.

US President Donald Trump said on Monday the bombers were moved because “there were some threats”, which he believed were linked to Iran. “So we moved them around a little bit, not very far,” he told reporters at the White House.

Hours earlier, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio played down any link to the alleged plot, saying it was “not unusual to see rotations happen” and that he had confidence in the security of US bases.

What happened at RAF Fairford?

On September 27, police arrested five men on suspicion of plotting to plant explosives near Fairford in the United Kingdom. They were released on bail a day later.

Investigators found petrol but no explosive devices in their vans, though UK officials say the men remain under investigation. On Thursday, police arrested a 25-year-old UK-Iranian dual national in London on suspicion of plotting an attack on the airbase. He was also released on bail on October 3.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham suggested that “Iran played a part” in the alleged plot but declined to give details. Iran has denied any such scheme and summoned the UK ambassador in Tehran in protest at the arrests.

What bombers does the US have?

The US Air Force flies three types of bombers, with a fourth on the way.

The B-52 Stratofortress is the oldest. The B-52H model currently in service was built in the early 1960s. With a wingspan of 56 metres (185 feet), it is the largest US bomber and can carry about 31 tonnes of weapons, including nuclear bombs and cruise missiles.

The B-1B Lancer, which entered service in the mid-1980s, is the fastest of the three. It can reach 1.2 times the speed of sound and has a swing-wing that sweeps back for high-speed flight. It carries the largest conventional payload, about 34 tonnes, but no longer carries nuclear weapons. These were the aircraft that left Fairford.

The B-2 Spirit is a flying-wing stealth bomber designed to slip past air defences. Only 20 were built, of which 19 remain in service. It can carry both nuclear and conventional weapons, including the 13,600kg (30,000lb) “bunker buster” bomb used in US strikes on Iran’s nuclear sites in June 2025.

The B-21 Raider, a smaller stealth bomber, is still in flight testing, and it remains on track for delivery in 2027. Over the next decade and a half, the air force plans to replace the B-1B and B-2, leaving a future fleet of B-21s and upgraded B-52s.

Where do these bombers fly from?

All US bombers are permanently based in the US, at five main airbases:

  • B-52H: Barksdale Air Force Base in Louisiana and Minot Air Force Base in North Dakota
  • B-1B: Dyess Air Force Base in Texas and Ellsworth Air Force Base in South Dakota
  • B-2: Whiteman Air Force Base in Missouri
  • B-21: Due to arrive at Ellsworth in South Dakota in 2027

All of these bases have long, wide runways, typically exceeding 10,000 feet (3,048 metres).

That makes bomber runways about as long as those at a big international airport. What limits where bombers can operate is not tarmac but security, weapons storage and support.

For missions abroad, the US rotates bombers through a handful of forward bases. Other important overseas operating locations include Andersen Air Force Base in Guam and Diego Garcia in the Indian Ocean.

Beyond these, the air force sends small groups of bombers to allied airbases for a few weeks at a time, in what it calls Bomber Task Force deployments. Recent rotations have included B-52s at Moron in Spain, B-1Bs at Orland in Norway and Misawa in Japan, and B-52s at Tindal in northern Australia, which arrived in September.

The bombers can also go on a strike mission from the US with the help of aerial refuelling. Bomber missions during the US-Israel war on Iran lasted more than 30 hours there and back. Each group of three bombers needed six to nine tanker aircraft to refuel them along the way.

entries.title: Pakistan, Turkiye join Saudi deterrence against Houthis: What that means
entries.summary: Islamabad says its role is defensive, but Riyadh's offensive in Yemen tests how long it can stay out of the fight.
entries.content:
Islamabad says its role is defensive, but Riyadh’s offensive in Yemen tests how long it can stay out of the fight.

Islamabad, Pakistan — For the first time since it was signed in August, the Mecca pact between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye is now in force.

At an emergency meeting in Riyadh on Monday, the pact’s top committee agreed to deploy Pakistani and Turkish forces to the kingdom as Saudi Arabia backs an offensive against Yemen’s Houthis.

“The Committee decided to move immediately to the practical implementation of the collective defense commitments and to take the necessary measures to provide the agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the Kingdom, in accordance with the approved arrangements and the national legislation of the Parties,” said a joint statement shared by Pakistan’s Foreign Office.

The statement did not specify the size or role of the forces.

Saudi-led coalition spokesperson Major General Turki al-Malki said 100 fighter jets were supporting a Yemeni government counteroffensive to retake territory seized by the Houthis last month.

Hours after the meeting, Pakistan’s Defence Minister Khawaja Asif said Pakistani forces were already playing a part.

“The forces of Turkiye and Pakistan are playing a supporting role. We are definitely involved in reconnaissance and such things, but the combat is practically being conducted by Saudi Arabia’s own forces, and they are the ones retaking those areas,” Asif told Geo News, speaking from Riyadh on Monday night.

That leaves Pakistan in a defensive role alongside a Saudi offensive. Analysts told Al Jazeera that it raises a question Islamabad has yet to answer publicly: How long it can stay out of the actual fighting?

What is already in place?

Pakistan’s military presence in Saudi Arabia is not new. It has trained Saudi military personnel since 1967, with a 1982 agreement formalising the deputation of troops to the kingdom.

A declassified CIA assessment from June 1985 estimated that 13,000 to 14,000 Pakistanis were serving in the Saudi army, including an armoured brigade at Tabuk. During the 1990-91 Gulf War, Pakistan also sent a large contingent to the kingdom for defensive duties.

Pakistan also signed a Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement with Saudi Arabia in September 2025, which treats aggression against either country as aggression against both.

In April, Riyadh confirmed that a Pakistani force, including fighter and support aircraft, had arrived at King Abdulaziz airbase in the Eastern Province.

Pakistan has never disclosed how many of its troops are in Saudi Arabia.

In September, Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry, director general of the military’s media wing, Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), told the Saudi outlet Arab News that Pakistani forces were already deployed to protect the kingdom and its holy sites.

“I would like to underscore here the word ‘physically’,” Chaudhry said. “We will go to any extent.”

ISPR did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment on the deployment agreed in Riyadh.

On Tuesday, Pakistan’s Ministry of Information said in a post on X that the country’s commitment to the security of the holy sites and the kingdom was not negotiable.

“The operational details of the actualisation of the collective deterrence are a matter of operational confidentiality and may not be made subject of media speculation,” the ministry said.

Turkiye’s footprint is less clear.

Asif said Turkish forces were also present, but Ankara has not publicly confirmed any deployment.

“There is no publicly acknowledged standing Turkish deployment in Saudi Arabia,” Gokhan Ereli, an international relations expert at Istanbul’s Ibn Haldun University, told Al Jazeera.

Ereli noted that under Article 92 of Turkiye’s constitution, the authority to send troops abroad rests with parliament, which has yet to ratify the Mecca pact.

What could deterrence look like?

Dania Thafer, executive director of the Gulf International Forum, said Riyadh wants the pact to carry real weight.

“Saudi Arabia is trying to turn the Mecca Pact from a political declaration into a deterrent,” she told Al Jazeera.

For now, she said, Riyadh mainly wants Pakistan and Turkiye to help defend Saudi territory and reinforce its air and missile defences, showing that another attack is no longer only a Saudi-Houthi matter. The Houthis have attacked multiple Saudi cities and facilities, including the East West Pipeline that Riyadh has been using to export oil amid Iranian restrictions on transit through the Strait of Hormuz during the ongoing war waged by the US.

Saudi authorities said two of its airports had been hit on Monday evening, injuring at least three people.

But Saudi Defence Minister Khalid bin Salman’s account of the meeting went further than what Thafer suggested.

“The committee agreed to activate collective deterrence measures within the framework of the Alliance in response to the attacks and all those responsible for them,” he wrote on X.

Thafer said the wording was deliberate.

“‘All those responsible’ is intentionally ambiguous. It tells the Houthis that Saudi Arabia may go beyond intercepting missiles and strike any actor or infrastructure enabling those attacks. It is also simultaneously warning external sponsors that Riyadh is watching the entire support network,” she said.

However, Pakistani officials have been more cautious.

“The document itself says, first, that it is defensive in nature. It has no offensive agenda,” Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said at a news conference in Islamabad on October 2.

Tughral Yamin, a retired brigadier and senior associate at Islamabad’s Institute of Policy Studies, said Pakistan’s contribution was likely to be specialised rather than large.

“Pakistan is most likely going to beef up its existing presence with air defence units, drones, battlefield communication systems and offensive cyber specialists, men from the corps of engineers to lay and lift mines, some special service troops. Nothing more than that, I would say,” he told Al Jazeera.

Ereli expects Turkiye’s role to be similarly limited.

“The realistic response would be calibrated and mostly non-ground. That means diplomatic coordination, intelligence sharing, emergency resupply of air defence, drones and electronic warfare, and perhaps naval or air-defence assets,” he said.

Could it extend into Yemen?

Thafer said two campaigns were now running side by side.

“There are really two concentric operations taking place: one is defending Saudi Arabia; the second is changing the military balance inside Yemen so the Houthis cannot continue attacking Saudi territory from a position of growing strength,” she said.

Pakistan has not said publicly where its role stops.

Asked by reporters in Rome on September 30 whether Pakistani forces had joined strikes in Yemen, Asif did not answer directly.

“I’m not going into detail, but obviously when I say that we are bound by this arrangement to defend Saudi Arabia, that means whatever means are available at our disposal, they’ll be available to Saudi Arabia also,” he said.

Pakistan has faced this question before.

In April 2015, its parliament unanimously resolved that “Pakistan should maintain neutrality in the Yemen conflict so as to be able to play a proactive diplomatic role to end the crisis”. But the resolution also pledged that Pakistan would stand with Saudi Arabia if its territorial integrity were violated or the holy sites threatened.

Monday’s joint statement justified the deployment in similar terms and condemned the attempted targeting of Mecca and Medina.

Tehran, though, is watching closely. On Sunday, Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said Tehran hoped reports of a Pakistani deployment for war in Yemen were untrue. He warned that any new intervention would only complicate the situation.

At the same news conference last week, Dar said he had raised the pact with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi in New York in September, on the margins of the United Nations General Assembly.

“I made them aware that we are in a defence pact, and as Muslims we have to honour it, and God willing, we will,” he said.

He said the Iranian leaders had suggested engaging the Houthis politically rather than through military action. Monday’s statement made no mention of a political track.

Javad Heiran-Nia, an analyst with the Persian Gulf Studies Group in Tehran, said Iran draws a clear distinction.

“In general, if Pakistan’s deployment is purely defensive and limited to the protection of Saudi installations, Tehran can tolerate it. However, if Pakistan joins offensive operations against the Houthis, Iran regards it as a red line, since it views the Houthis as part of its strategic depth in the Arabian Peninsula,” he told Al Jazeera.

“Currently, Pakistan’s mediation has shifted from neutrality to management of conflicting interests, and its credibility is highly fragile,” he added.

Yamin, too, said the onus was on Islamabad.

“Pakistan needs to draw its redlines carefully to prevent its troops getting involved in combat operations against the Houthis. So the question should [be] not how will they get involved but how can they prevent getting involved,” he said.

How long will it last?

Much depends on what Riyadh wants from Yemen.

“Riyadh probably wants a short, high-intensity campaign that restores deterrence rather than another open-ended Yemen war,” Thafer said.

But Yemeni government forces this week said they were no longer limiting their ambitions to regaining territory lost to the Houthis in recent weeks, and were in fact aiming to retake capital Sanaa, held by the Iran-backed group since 2014.

“Military campaigns are determined by objectives: securing Saudi territory and Bab al-Mandab could potentially be limited,” Thafer said. “Trying to fundamentally defeat the Houthis or retake Sanaa would be a very different and potentially much longer war.”

entries.title: Qatar and India among seven countries bidding for 2036 Olympics, IOC says
entries.summary: South Africa, Turkiye, Germany, Hungary and South Korea are on the list of countries revealed by the IOC.
entries.content:
South Africa, Turkiye, Germany, Hungary and South Korea are in the list of countries revealed by the IOC.

Qatar’s bid to host the 2036 Summer Olympics has been confirmed by the International Olympic Committee (IOC), which said India was also among the seven countries in the running.

South Africa, Germany, Hungary, Turkiye and South Korea make up the rest of the current list issued by the IOC on Tuesday.

Other countries have until October 31 to declare an interest.

Qatar hosted the 2022 football World Cup and was home to the 2006 Asian Games, which it will host again in 2030.

In March 2027, the IOC Executive Board will draw up a shortlist of the interested parties, who will then enter dialogue with the Olympic body.

The IOC said the 2036 hosts would be assessed on factors such as funding and political and public support.

“Wherever the Games take place, one thing must never change: Athletes have to be at the heart of everything we do,” IOC President Kirsty Coventry said in a statement.

“That is why, for every future host, delivering the best possible experience for the athletes must always be the starting point,” the Zimbabwean former swimmer added.

India has stated its intention to host an Olympics for the first time, centred on Ahmedabad, the key city in Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s home state of Gujarat.

Ahmedabad will host the 2030 multisport Commonwealth Games, seen as a major rehearsal for an Olympics. The city is also home to the world’s largest cricket stadium.

South Africa hosted the 2010 football World Cup and the 1995 Rugby World Cup but has never played host to an Olympics.

An Olympics in the Gulf would have to be moved to later than its traditional July-August slot due to the heat.

The German National Olympic Committee voted last month to select Munich as its candidate city for a Games that will take place a century after the infamous 1936 Berlin Olympics, which were overseen by the Nazi regime.

The Turkish Olympic authorities hope to do one better than in the bidding for the 2020 Summer Olympics, when Istanbul came second to Tokyo.

The 2028 Summer Olympics will take place in Los Angeles, while Brisbane has been awarded the 2032 edition.

Preferred hosts ⁠⁠will be named in ⁠⁠2028, and a final decision is expected in mid-2029, the IOC said.

entries.title: Tennis: World number one Sinner will not play in 2026 due to knee injury
entries.summary: Jannik Sinner has not competed in a tournament since winning at Wimbledon in July and will continue his recovery.
entries.content:
Jannik Sinner has not competed in a tournament since winning at Wimbledon in July and will continue his recovery.

World number one men’s tennis player Jannik Sinner will not compete again in 2026 after opting to continue his recovery from a knee injury that has kept him out of action since his triumphant Wimbledon campaign in July.

The five-time Grand Slam winner will “follow a course of treatment for inflammation in his knee”, Sinner’s team said in a statement on Tuesday.

“The decision has been made to have the treatment now to give Jannik the necessary time to recover before beginning preparations for 2027. As a result, Jannik will be unable to compete again during the 2026 season.”

Sinner also posted the update on his personal Instagram account, where he recounted ending last year on a high after retaining his ATP Finals title in Turin as he battled past then world number one Carlos Alcaraz.

“But at the moment, I also need to think about my long-term career,” he said in a video posted on Instagram.

“I will do everything possible to get back to 100 percent [and] I hope to see you very, very soon on court again.”

Sinner, 25, has not played since his triumph at the All England ⁠⁠Club, missing the North American hardcourt swing, including the US Open, and the ongoing ATP 500 event in Beijing.

He announced last week that he was withdrawing from the Shanghai Masters, which he won in 2024 after defeating Novak Djokovic in the final.

Now he will also miss the Paris Masters and the ATP Finals in November. Plus, he will not be able to play for Italy, the host nation and three-time defending champion, in the Davis Cup Final 8.

Sinner risks losing the top ranking while he’s out.

But if Sinner does return at the start of next year, he could play the Australian Open – the next Grand Slam – which starts January 17.

He enjoyed a 30-match winning streak this year before his meltdown in a second-round defeat at the French Open amid a Paris heatwave.

Sinner’s main rival missed four and a half months this year due to a right wrist injury.

Meanwhile, Germany’s Alexander Zverev won two of the four Grand Slam titles and is nearing the No 1 ranking.

entries.title: How Palestinian reporters defied Israel’s genocide to redefine journalism
entries.summary: Western media under scrutiny for promoting Israeli narrative rather than standing up for vulnerable journalists in Gaza.
entries.content:
Western media have come under scrutiny for buying into the Israeli narrative rather than standing up for vulnerable journalists in Gaza and elsewhere.

Israel has killed about 250 journalists since launching its genocidal war on Gaza on October 7, 2023. That is more than the number of journalists killed in all wars in the past 150 years combined.

The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) says Israel has engaged in “the deadliest and most deliberate effort to kill and silence journalists” that the media watchdog has ever documented.

Jonathan Dagher, the head of Reporters Without Borders’ Middle East desk, called the targeting of journalists “a tragedy for journalism”, while the United Nations human rights chief, Volker Turk, called Gaza “a ‘death trap’ for journalists”.

Yet, beyond the statements and condolences, Israel has never been held accountable for its killing of Palestinian journalists – a practice that long predates the genocidal war on Gaza, but that took on an industrial scale over the past three years.

Instead, the silence of the international community and lack of solidarity from Western media professionals emboldened Israel as it pursued the genocidal war and normalised journalists’ killings.

But despite trying to suppress the truth about its massacres and attempts at ethnic cleansing, Israel – historically an acknowledged master at propaganda – has largely failed in its efforts over the past three years, thanks to the bravery of the very voices it tried to silence.

That too is the story of how journalism has changed since October 7, 2023.

‘Neutral’ amid genocide

Western media outlets and their prominent faces often claimed to be “neutral” in their coverage of the genocidal war.

But the very concept of neutrality in journalism has come under question amid the genocide.

The Western media were rarely neutral when viewed according to the basic tenets of journalism and professional standards. More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza so far. But Western outlets often framed headlines in the passive tense when reporting on these killings, conveniently shielding Israel from blame.

Palestinians were killed by Israel, mostly in circumstances that violated rules of war. These details were not highlighted, and the Israeli narrative that Hamas was using Palestinian civilians as a “human shield” was amplified.

When Al Jazeera journalist Anas al-Sharif was killed in a targeted attack in front of al-Shifa Hospital in August 2025, CNN carried the Israeli accusation that he worked for a Hamas cell in its second paragraph, an allegation Al Jazeera has rejected.

Weeks before the killing, Irene Khan, the UN’s special rapporteur on freedom of opinion and expression, had warned against “repeated threats and accusations” against al-Sharif by the Israeli army.

Israel killed 22 people, including five journalists – one of whom worked for Al Jazeera – in a “double-tap” strike in September 2025. It claimed that it had targeted a “Hamas camera.” Most media outlets ran the story. The Reuters news agency, whose journalist was also killed in the attack, confirmed that the camera belonged to it.

Similarly, when Israel targeted media personnel in Lebanon early in the war, a Sky News post on X called it a hit on a “Hezbollah-linked” broadcaster.

Israel has also been accused of jailing and torturing Palestinian journalists for doing their job. During the genocidal war, it has tried to control the narrative domestically too, cracking down on Haaretz for its critical coverage of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s failures on October 7, 2023, and the atrocities in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.

The Netanyahu government imposed a ban on Al Jazeera, calling the network a security threat. Al Jazeera described the shutdown as a “criminal act” and warned that Israel’s suppression of the free press “stands in contravention of international and humanitarian law”.

This was not the first time Al Jazeera has been targeted. In 2021, a Gaza building housing Al Jazeera’s office was destroyed in an Israeli missile strike. Israel has killed many Al Jazeera journalists even before October 2023.

Shireen Abu Akleh, considered a voice of Palestine, was killed by an Israeli soldier while she was reporting in the occupied West Bank in 2022. Her killer was never charged for the murder.

Assal Rad, an activist and Middle East historian, has accused the Western media of enabling attacks on journalists.

“When you’re repeating what Israel says, you’re creating space to legitimise the targeting of their own colleagues,” she said in an interview with Columbia Journalism Review on September 30.

Double standards

While reporting on Russian aggression against Ukraine, media around the world rightly humanised the victims.

But that same journalistic standard was missing, far too often, when Western outlets reported on Palestinians killed by Israel. Instead, they were at times portrayed as collateral damage, their deaths the result of fighting between two sides.

Israel has killed more than 21,000 children in Gaza in the last three years. But the faces of thousands of babies, children and mothers, and their suffering and despair, were frequently buried under statistics. They were nameless, faceless, their lives and stories deemed unworthy of human treatment.

Moreover, Western reporting often lacked historical contextualisation, erasing the history of Israel’s brutal occupation, territorial expansion and the ethnic cleansing of Palestinians. More than 750,000 Palestinians were expelled or displaced from their homes, leading up to the formation of Israel in 1948. Israel has since forcibly displaced more Palestinians from the occupied territory.

Israeli leaders now publicly oppose the establishment of Palestinian statehood as part of the so-called two-state solution and successive governments have expanded illegal settlements on Palestinian lands.

Western media often present settler violence and government-backed illegal settlement expansion as separate, when in fact, the Israeli government has armed, funded and granted impunity to those involved.

Fundamentally, treating Israel – an occupying power in Gaza and the West Bank – and Palestinians as equal sides is itself problematic. It is not objective journalism; it is far from it. It misses the asymmetry inherent in this equation. On the one hand is a major military power in illegal occupation of another people’s land, waging a genocidal war on them and seeking to ethnically cleanse them; on the other is a Palestinian resistance movement consisting of multiple strands united only in their struggle to achieve self-determination, a right guaranteed under the UN Charter.

Objectivity requires that news reports highlight Israel’s use of disproportionate force and the firing of banned weapons at civilian areas – violations of the rules of war and war crimes. Instead, Palestinian experts and commentators were the ones grilled and pressed to condemn Hamas as a condition for even being heard.

The challenge

Still, the Western media’s lopsided coverage did not go unchallenged. It triggered rebellion in several newsrooms, including the BBC and The New York Times.

More than 1,500 Western journalists from various news organisations signed an open letter in protest against the coverage of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. Eight BBC journalists wrote an open letter, accusing the broadcaster of failing to accurately report on the Israel-Palestine conflict.

They accused their organisation of running with pro-Israel editorial biases, downplaying Palestinian casualties and suppressing terms like “genocide”, “apartheid” or “occupation”. Many journalists of colour resigned in protest.

This has dented the credibility of Western media’s reporting on critical international issues at a time of global upheaval.

However, the unprecedented Israeli attacks on journalists did not deter Palestinians from reporting. They risked their lives to get the story out via social media, especially TikTok and Instagram.

“They take revenge on us through our children? It doesn’t matter. We will stay. We will continue. This is our path, and we chose it knowingly. We will not stop,” said Wael al-Dahdouh, Al Jazeera Arabic’s then-Gaza bureau chief, after Israel killed his wife, daughter, two sons, and a grandson in separate Israeli air strikes.

People across the world, including young Americans who primarily consume news on social media, were horrified by the graphic images coming out of Palestine despite the efforts of legacy media outlets to sanitise the Gaza genocide.

It triggered student protests at Columbia University that soon spread to other campuses.

Palestinian journalists became “the eyes of Gaza”, showing the world what rights organisations dubbed Israel’s “livestreamed genocide” against Palestinians.

One of them, Bisan Owda, who won an Emmy Award for her reporting on daily life and survival during the genocidal war on Gaza, is known for her resilience as a Palestinian journalist.

“Hello, my name is Bisan, and I am still alive…” became Owda’s signature greeting in her social media posts.

“I no longer have any dreams. My only dream is to survive this, to tell the story of the people who didn’t,” she said on the 27th day of the genocidal war.

She and hundreds of Palestinian journalists have done just that. In the process, they have upended a media landscape where giant organisations beholden to power have long controlled who gets to be heard and seen.

Ultimately, Israel’s genocide in Gaza has also been a war on truth. Thanks to Owda and her Palestinian colleagues, that is a war Israel has lost.

entries.title: Russia plague quarantine following lab death: Should we be worried?
entries.summary: Plague is still endemic to Siberia, the location of the first known prehistoric human outbreak.
entries.content:
Plague is still endemic to Siberia, the location of the first known prehistoric human outbreak.

Dozens of people have been quarantined in Russia’s Siberia after a laboratory worker at a plague research institute fell ill and died in undisclosed circumstances.

Russian news outlet People of Baikal reported the woman may have contracted pneumonic plague from a broken test tube and died.

Plague is a severe, life-threatening infection caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. Between 1346 and 1353, the bubonic plague – one of three forms of the disease – was known as the Black Death. It caused one of the most fatal pandemics in the world across Eurasia and North Africa. Some 30-60 percent of the population of Europe is believed to have died in that outbreak.

Pneumonic plague is less common than bubonic plague. It is a severe form of the infection that can spread from person to person.

What happened in the Russian lab and should we be worried?

Here’s what we know:

What happened in the Russian lab?

On Monday, Russian media reported that a 28-year-old woman named Darya Shipilova, who had been working at the Irkutsk Anti-plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, died from suspected pneumonic plague last week.

According to Russian media reports, Shipilova became ill while at work on September 30 and died two days later at a hospital in the nearby town of Shelekhov. Several media reports suggest there may have been an accident at the lab, but this has not been officially confirmed.

About 200 people who came into contact with the dead woman have since been quarantined, and parts of the hospital where she died have also been cordoned off. An aluminium plant nearby has instructed its workers to wear masks.

Anna Popova, head of Russia’s public health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, flew to Irkutsk to meet with Governor Igor Kobzev and other officials four days ago.

In a statement quoted by the TASS news agency, Rospotrebnadzor said officials in the Irkutsk region had detected two cases ⁠of COVID and two cases of rhinoviruses among people who had been in contact with the researcher. No other cases of infectious diseases were noted.

Later on Monday, Russian authorities said they found no evidence that the woman’s illness was caused by any of the pathogens she worked with and said the situation was under control.

Kobzev said in ⁠a statement that the woman had died of “pneumonia of unknown aetiology”, adding: “Importantly, over the past few days, no new cases of staff from the Anti-Plague Institute seeking medical attention have been identified.”

He added that the situation was under control and that all known contacts with the dead woman had been identified, examined and placed under medical supervision.

What is plague and what are its symptoms?

The bacterium which causes plague, Yersinia pestis, is carried by small wild mammals and their fleas. In Siberia, where it is endemic, it is rare for Russians to fall ill with the plague, however. But cases occur every year in other parts of the world, notably in Africa.

According to the Centres for Disease Control (CDC) in the US, plague has been detected in people of all ages, from babies to those aged in their 90s. Half of the cases occur in people aged 12 to 45. Men and women are susceptible, although it has been slightly more common among men.

There are three main types of plague, affecting different parts of the body. These are bubonic, septicaemic and pneumonic. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), bubonic plague is the most common clinical form. Symptoms include painful swollen lymph nodes or “buboes”.

Septicaemic plague infects the blood while pneumonic plague affects the lungs.

The WHO describes septicaemic and pneumonic plague as “less common, but severe forms” of plague.

A fourth type, pharyngeal plague, is rare. It can be contracted by eating infected meat.

According to the US-based Cleveland Clinic, besides swollen lymph nodes in the case of bubonic plague, those infected can display the following symptoms:

  • Fever and chills.
  • Headaches and body aches.
  • Weakness and fatigue.
  • Dizziness.
  • Nausea.
  • Vomiting and diarrhoea.

Complications can arise from plague if it is untreated, according to the Cleveland Clinic. These include:

  • Meningitis – a severe infection that causes inflammation of the lining of the brain and spinal cord.
  • Tissue death and loss of limbs from gangrene.
  • Respiratory failure.
  • Organ failure.

Bubonic plague has a death rate of 30 to 60 percent. Pneumonic and septicaemic plague are fatal if left untreated within one to six days, the WHO says.

If identified quickly, however, all forms can be treated with antibiotics.

How does plague spread?

Plague most commonly spreads through the bites of fleas carried by rodents, but can also be transmitted from person to person.

According to the CDC in the US, people can also become infected through exposure to sick pets, especially cats.

These are the main ways the disease can be transmitted:

Flea bites

According to the CDC, people and animals can contract plague from dead rats carrying the disease, as well as being bitten by fleas that have bitten infected rats. “Dogs and cats may also bring plague-infected fleas into the home. Flea bite exposure may result in primary bubonic plague or septicemic plague,” the CDC states.

Direct contact

Humans can contract plague through contact with the tissue or body fluids of an infected animal. This form of exposure most commonly results in bubonic plague or septicaemic plague, according to the CDC.

Infectious droplets

Droplets coughed out by humans and animals infected with pneumonic plague can hang in the air and be inhaled by another person. The CDC states that this requires direct and close contact with the person or animal with pneumonic plague, and it is the only way the disease can be transmitted from person to person.

According to the CDC, the last documented case of person-to-person pneumonic plague transmission was in 1924. However, there have been more recent cases of pneumonic plague transmitted to humans by sick cats.

“Cats are particularly susceptible to plague and can be infected by eating infected rodents. Cats with plague pose a risk of transmitting infectious plague droplets to their owners or to veterinarians,” the CDC states.

Where does plague exist?

Ian Jones, professor of virology at the University of Reading, told The Associated Press news agency that “plague carries a huge history and is still present in many parts of the world, including Russia.”

Worldwide, there are between 1,000 and 2,000 cases of plague every year, according to Cleveland Clinic in the US.

Plague is endemic to Siberia, which is the location of the first known prehistoric human outbreak. Besides Russia, plague is also endemic in several countries, according to the WHO. Between 2019 and 2025, most new cases recorded by the WHO occurred in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Madagascar.

There have been rare cases elsewhere. In July 2025, an Arizona man who worked with cats died of pneumonic plague – the first such death since 2007.

There was a major outbreak of bubonic plague in Los Angeles in 1924-1925, after it was first recorded in the US in 1900, brought by infected rats on steamships. Bubonic plague has made up 80 percent of an average of seven cases per year in the US since then. Most of these have occurred in northern New Mexico, northern Arizona, southern Colorado, California, southern Oregon and western Nevada, according to the CDC.

Why has this incident triggered global alarm?

While authorities in Russia have stressed that postmortem tests carried out on the woman did not detect that she had plague, the incident has raised global alarm.

Several authorities have called on Russia to give more clarity about what exactly happened to the woman at the lab.

In Washington, United States President Donald Trump said he was watching the situation with concern and that the US would be willing to help, though he said he had not spoken to Russian President Vladimir Putin about the situation.

“It’s a rough disease. You know, that’s a disease we used to be able to control, but somehow those microbes have gotten stronger and smarter. They’re like an army,” Trump told reporters outside the White House.

“Even with great advancement, the germs have really become relatively stronger than they were, and things that used to work on pneumonia don’t work as well any more,” he added.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Monday that he does not believe there is cause for alarm, but that the US is watching the case closely, aware that “it could spread quickly” despite the quarantine and other public health protocols.

Should the world be worried?

On Monday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the public and media should follow official statements from Rospotrebnadzor, rather than “rumours or speculation”.

“It is difficult to comment with confidence given the relatively limited information currently available,” Malick Gibani, clinical associate professor in bacterial vaccinology at Imperial College London, said in a statement to the media.

“Based on reports, there appears to be a suspected index case, and contacts have been quarantined. If there is an exposure in a laboratory to a potentially dangerous pathogen, the usual procedure would be to undertake a risk assessment of who may have been exposed and the nature of their contact.”

He added: “People considered at risk can then be monitored and, where appropriate, screening, quarantine, or post-exposure prophylaxis with antibiotics may be offered. I think it’s important that we see how this pans out, and ideally, there’d be good communication between the public health authorities and the wider global health community.

“I think this emphasises the need to be aware of ongoing outbreaks of serious bacterial pathogens and highlights the need for investment in biosecurity, particularly for preventing biological risks. This could include developing medical countermeasures like better diagnostics or vaccines,” Gibani said.

entries.title: India opposition leaders briefly arrested in protest against election chief
entries.summary: Protesters are demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
entries.content:
Protesters are demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

Police have briefly arrested several opposition legislators in New Delhi for trying to breach barricades during a protest march to demand the resignation of ⁠the election chief over a controversial revision of voter lists.

Rahul Gandhi, a leader of the Congress party, was among the lawmakers detained in the Indian capital on Tuesday, but was released soon after, the AFP news agency and local media reported.

The march is the latest in a series of near-daily protests beginning last week led by student groups, opposition parties and India’s “Cockroach” youth movement.

The protesters are demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, accusing the polling body he oversees of manipulating voter registrations to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party.

“The election commission is a puppet in the ‌hands of the government,” Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge told reporters as the march began.

“After failing multiple times, Congress leaders have decided to establish anarchy in ⁠the country and attack institutions,” BJP spokesperson Sambit Patra told reporters before Tuesday’s protest.

Lawmakers carried placards, waved the national flag, and shouted slogans against Kumar during the march, roughly 1km (0.6 miles) long, to the Election Commission headquarters from parliament, through the centre of New Delhi.

India began its Special Intensive Revision of voter lists in Bihar last year before state elections. The exercise has since expanded to most states and federally administered territories.

Critics say the process requires documents that are confusing and difficult to obtain, risking the exclusion of millions of eligible voters. Election Commission data shows voter rolls could shrink by as much as 30 percent in some regions.

The Election Commission says the voter-roll revision is designed to remove duplicate, deceased or ineligible entries and maintain electoral integrity. On Friday, it directed its officials to register eligible voters inadvertently omitted from electoral rolls.
